utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can hear the B/C/S translation very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please check the channels. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And now? Yes. Yes. Can you hear the English Channel now? One, two, three. One, two, three. One, two, three. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These things should be checked before the beginning of the hearing. Let us adjourn for a few minutes for the technician to arrive. So I'll give you the floor in a moment. We will suspend the hearing for a few minutes. --- Break taken at 9.03 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. So we can continue with the session. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence team once again so that they can introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. For the Defence of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. At the same time, Your Honour, for the sake of the transcript, I'd like to point out to the fact that on page 1 of the transcript yesterday, lines 19 and 20, there is a mistake in relation to the name of our legal assistant. Yesterday we had Muriel Cauvin, and the transcript says Mirna Milanovic. So could you please correct that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for specifying that and for making this correction. It will be taken on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution once again so they can introduce themselves once again, so for the sake of proper form do please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Mr. Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Thank you very much. So good day to all those present, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and all the rest of the staff in this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, in the future, it would be a good idea if you were able to check that the equipment works properly just before the start of the session so that we don't keep wasting ten minutes at the start of each session. Today we are meant to hear a witness, but before the arrival of the witness I wanted to specify one point in relation to what was said a couple of days ago with regard to the translation of some documents. The Trial Chamber expressed a wish - it's just a simple wish - but, to the extent possible, if you believe that the documents are very important and if you think that they may give rise to a discussion when they are shown to the witness and in the course of the cross-examination -- of course, the Defence may also make other points in relation to those documents. So to the extent to which it is possible, it would be a good idea for these documents to be translated into French as well. If you're unable to do that for technical reasons or whatever, at that stage, okay, we'll be working on the basis of the B/C/S document translated into English. But if it were at all possible, in order to save us time, do please make sure that you have the documents translated into French as well. But we do understand that in certain cases it may cause problems of cost or material difficulties in general. So okay, I just wanted to make that point. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is an important issue, and we understand that the Chamber is very well aware of the potential implications; namely, that it could be a potential ground for an appeal, and if successful, such an appeal would result in a retrial -- in a retrial of a trial which is scheduled for more than one year; and of a trial in which, at least from the Prosecution's side, more than 100 witnesses will be called. Mr. President, Your Honours, any - any - ambiguity must be avoided. The language on the records must be absolutely clear. The question, Mr. President, Your Honours, the question to answer is: Are all three Judges of this Bench - are you, Mr. Presiding Judge, are you, Judge Rasoazanany, and are you, Judge Swart - are you able to read and to understand English to the extent necessary to follow and to fully and comprehensively assess and to evaluate the evidence presented in the English language to decide on the guilt of the accused? There is only the answer yes or no. There is nothing in between. Mr. President, Your Honours, there is a certain background why I'm asking this. As you already mentioned, Mr. President, on 29 January - and I refer to the transcript - you, Mr. President, said - and this is a quote - "Therefore, an important document that is tendered into evidence, if the evidence was originally in B/C/S, it should be translated into English and into French to allow the Chamber to fully appreciate the probative value, the relevance, and the weight of the document." And in Your Honour Judge Rasoazanany's official ICTY CV is written -- is written under the section "Languages," "French, conversational English." Again, Mr. President, Your Honours, the question is: Are all three Judges of this Bench able to read and understand English to the extent necessary to fully and comprehensively assess and to evaluate the evidence presented in the English language to decide on the guilt of the accused? I would appreciate, Your Honour, if you would like to finish me, it would take me just one -- one more minute. This is a very serious issue. If the answer is no, I already announce now that the Prosecution will - and it may be joined by the Defence or not - but the Prosecution will apply for an adjournment of proceedings in order to get all - and I repeat, to get all - documents translated into the French language. Due to the volume of the documentary evidence, it can be anticipated that such an adjournment would last for a number of months. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, the Trial Chamber cannot but be surprised by your words. I would like to tell you that when this matter of translation was raised, the main reason was that most documents are in the B/C/S. According to the list coming from the Prosecution, these B/C/S documents are translated into English. Yesterday I pointed out that the English translation of a document which was tendered into evidence was already a problem, to the extent that the translation went beyond the contents of the original B/C/S text. In order to be able to assess the value, the probational value [as interpreted] of this document and to be able to assess the merits of the two texts, well, if we look at the -- all the versions, it makes it possible to us to properly judge the contents of the document. As I have mentioned, if it is not possible to proceed and have these texts translated into French as well, we shall continue to work on the basis of the B/C/S and English texts. However, if a text which is either in English or in B/C/S were to require a more in-depth analysis in relation to the scope of the sentences and the interpretation of the sentences included in that text, we could organise this interpretation through the registrar, its translation into French, in order to make proper comparisons. We have seen over the past few months that the problems pertaining to these translations in certain cases led to difficulties, since when witnesses speak B/C/S what they say is interpreted into English and French. And when we compare what was said and what we see on the transcript, sometimes we see slight differences, which means that in certain cases your handling of languages may lead to difficulties. If you do have difficulties, you would then always have the possibility of resorting to a specialised translation or some other practical solution. So far we have never had any problems with this. It is my impression that the Prosecution has not quite grasped the meaning of my comments in relation to the fact that we would wish to have translations into both English and French. I have mentioned this simply in order to save time in the course of our sessions. However, the fact remains that when the text is submitted in English, the Judges are fully capable of appreciating and assessing the text properly. So I fail to understand the meaning of your comments just now. So we are going to continue. So far we've never had any problems with this. But following the comment made by the Prosecution, I would like to hear what the Defence has to say. So I give the floor to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have listened to what you had to say. We base our considerations on the Statute; that is to say, both languages are equal before the Court. We don't know what the technical possibilities are for the secretariat to have the documents we submit translated into French, but to the extent to which we feel this is likely to contribute to a fair trial and a swift proceedings, the Defence will try and stick to your instructions. Unfortunately, Mr. President, I must say that in the first case when I came here in 1996 and - he working language was French but the situation here before the Court is such that the English language seems to prevail. So I myself had to go and learn some English. So the way I see it, yes, we'll try and do as you say, but obviously the English versions, the English translations, will prevail. Apart from that, Mr. President, I believe this was only one of quite a few procedural issues. I mean, this is still in the beginning of the trial. I suppose it should have been discussed in a different way, not quite in the way in which my honourable friend has done just now. But maybe there should have been a Status Conference where we could have discussed this and similar issues which have not been clarified as yet. So in that respect, the Defence teams - the two Defence teams - will -- I would like to suggest a Status Conference or an extra session where we could discuss all these procedural issues. And we would like to get some guidance from the Trial Chamber as to how to proceed so as to avoid any such misunderstandings in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the points of procedure, what point are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the communication that we've had so far between the two Defence teams, we have jotted down about three or four issues. We would like to suggest that in writing, and then it will be up to the Trial Chamber whether we have a Status Conference or not. As you might know, we raised some of these issues in the very beginning, and some of them have already been solved. It is about cross-examination, about second-hand evidence, and some other issues where perhaps we don't have fully specified rules. We have noticed that there are two or three other similar issues. We will submit our comments in writing. And if the Trial Chamber believes that they should listen to what both sides have to say on these points, in that case we would like to have a separate Status Conference so that we can discuss all these points and for the Trial Chamber to give us some guidance as to how to proceed in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the translation issue, for the Defence team for Mr. Kubura, we will certainly endeavour, Your Honour, within our means, to translate as many of the documents we will rely upon and the documents we regard as key into the French language in order to ensure proper respect for the Tribunal's official languages, which are both French and English. So we will endeavour to do whatever we can in that regard. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Dixon. As to the Status Conference, we shall see about it and we'll let you know. Now we can proceed to hear the witness. And I'm going to ask Madam Registrar to bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Can you hear me in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called to appear as a Prosecution witness. In order to do that, please tell me your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ivan Josipovic, and I was born on the 29th of November, 1957 in Mehurici, Travnik municipality. I'm currently living in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a graduate lawyer. I am currently retired and unemployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, some ten years ago, what were you doing? What was your occupation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add a couple of sentences. I completed elementary and secondary school in Vitez. I graduated at the School of Law in Zenica, which is a department of Sarajevo University. Upon graduation in 1975 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not my question. I'm not asking you about your studies. I'm asking you about your occupation. You told us that today you were a lawyer, and I am asking you what your occupation was ten years ago. Were you a lawyer, a student, an unemployed person, or a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I wanted to tell you; that is, that before the outbreak of the war I worked in Vitez municipality as a clerk for property relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're going to testify, and to do that you have to take the solemn declaration. So will you please read the text given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you are a lawyer, it may be superfluous for me to say what I'm going to say, but I still wish to point out that you have taken a solemn declaration regarding your testimony, as you know that solemn declarations means that you must not make any false testimony. Should you do that, you could be prosecuted. And according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, it is provided that when answering questions, if there are any elements that may incriminate you, in that case you can say so. And one day these words cannot -- or these elements cannot be taken against you. This is also part of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Therefore, please answer questions as fully and precisely as possible. As you know, you will be answering questions put to you by representatives of the Prosecution, which are seated to your right. At the completion of what is known as the examination-in-chief, you will have to answer questions within the framework of the cross-examination by counsel for the Defence, who are seated to your left. And the three Judge in front of you, should the need arise, according to Rule 89, may put questions to you as well for clarification purposes. That is how this hearing will proceed. If you have any difficulties with a particular question, you can always ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. If you still find it difficult, you can address the Chamber, which is in charge of the proceedings. We will begin with the examination-in-chief. And for that purpose, I give the floor to the representative of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in what year did you graduate from the law faculty?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1985 in Zenica, which is a department of the Faculty of Law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly where you were employed between 1985 and the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're not receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a problem. The interpretation is not reaching us. Please repeat the question, and we will check.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell the Trial Chamber briefly where you were employed between 1985 and the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Upon graduation from the Faculty of Law, my first job was in Vitez municipality in the cadastre department. I was a clerk for property and legal issues. I worked there briefly, three to four months. And after that, in the same administrative bodies, I was moved to the post of inspector in the fiscal administration. I was a tax inspector, as it was called then. I worked there for about two years. After that, there was a vacancy for the magistrate's judge, and I was elected to that position. I held that position for about four to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. five years. After that, again there was a vacancy in the police station in Vitez, and I was appointed to the position Chief of Legal and Administrative Affairs. And I stayed in that position until the events that followed, that is, until the heightening of tensions between these two peoples. And this occurred towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Trial Chamber about the rise in tensions between the different communities in the Vitez area in the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to observe, and working as the head of the legal affairs department in the police station of Vitez, I noticed that between the chief of the police station in Vitez, who headed the police station at the time - and his name was Pero Skopljak - whereas, the head of the uniformed police was Saban Mahmutovic. And judging by the way the reserve force of the police was organised, I noticed that both gentlemen sought to arm as many persons as possible with military equipment, uniforms. And I was able to see this on the basis of the number of booklets that were issued through the department that I was working in. This was my personal conclusion, that already at that time inter-ethnic relations were disrupted and tensions increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during the time that you were the head of the legal affairs and administrative department in the Vitez police department, did you have any contact or involvement with foreign fighters?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I had no contact whatsoever during that period of time while I was at the head of the legal and administrative department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any involvement with foreign fighters at a later point in time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When sometime in November I joined the HVO - that is, the military police of the 4th Battalion of the Vitez HVO - as an investigator, I did have occasion to have contact with certain foreigners who came to our area, both individually and in small groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your primary duties as an investigator with the military police of the 4th Battalion of the Vitez HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer and investigator in the 4th Battalion, my main duty was to investigate all criminal offences that may occur in the area that was under the control of the HVO and which were committed by HVO troops. These were mostly acts of burglary, theft, break-ins, self-inflicted wounds, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you have the opportunity to investigate any crimes allegedly committed by ABiH forces against Croat civilians, such as in Dusina or Maljine?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I personally did not, nor was I aware that any one of my colleagues in the 4th Battalion was assigned to going to Maljine or Dusina to investigate those acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As this area was under the control of the Army and Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was dangerous to go there and to make any kind of notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness, in the summer of 1993 when you were detained at a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 7th of August, 1993. As I was returning from duty, together with a colleague, and I intended to drop him off at Novi Travnik, which I did in fact. I left him there. And on my way back from Novi Travnik towards Vitez, at a crossroads of the Vitez-Travnik roads, I took a wrong turn, so that with my own passenger vehicle, a Golf, I turned left in the direction of Travnik believing I was driving towards Vitez. Not far from this crossroads, at a location called Kanare or Dolac, where there's a road turning off towards Guca Gora, I came across an obstacle on the road. I couldn't pass. I stopped. And just then I saw -- I realised that I had made a mistake and that I was in an area controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to the conclusion that you were in an area controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I stopped in my vehicle next to the obstacle, there were guards who consider securing the road and they were dressed in uniform and they had white belts, from which I concluded that they were members of the military police, because we, too, in the HVO wore similar belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any distinctive insignia on their uniforms that allowed you to determine which army or which unit of which army these military police belonged to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the military belts that they were wearing, they also had patches on their sleeves. On one arm, there were the lily patches. In those days, these were worn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army or which military unit wore patches, lily patches?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Such patches were worn by members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you stopped your vehicle at this checkpoint manned by ABiH military police officers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: After I was stopped, I was roughly pulled out of my car and -- one of them came up to me, opened the door, and pulled me out roughly from the car. And he shoved me into another vehicle that was standing nearby. And another one of them took my car and with these two vehicles - they were driving their own car and this other man, who was driving mine - we went not far from that spot, about 150 to 200 metres away to the building of an elementary school. I was taken there to the officer on duty. What exactly was his role, I cannot recollect now, but I know that I was brought before him and he asked me some routine questions, my name, where I was from. And then later he called up somebody on the phone - and I was later to learn that it was the Main Staff in Travnik - I was there for a very short period of time, after which I was driven to the barracks in Travnik, that is, the entrance of the barracks in Travnik, where they took me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, approximately what time on 7 August 1993 did you arrive at the barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to recollect exactly what time it was, but I think it was sometime in the evening, maybe around 10.00 in the evening. I may be wrong. It may have been a bit earlier than that. But anyway, between 9.00 and 10.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon your arrival at the main entrance to the Travnik barracks, did you see any soldiers at that point in time? And if so, were you able to determine what units or military organisation they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, when I arrived in front of the entrance to the barracks, I noticed that there were guards at the gates. They were again wearing uniforms with white belts, and just then I didn't know which unit they belonged to. I just noticed that they were wearing patches of the BH army -- with the lilies, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your arrival at the main entrance to the Travnik barracks, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: After I had passed through the gate itself, I was taken to a room at the very entrance to the barracks. It's a kind of hut which, as far as I can remember today, consisted of two or three rooms. And I was taken into one of them. And I was left there. Not for interrogation; I was simply taken inside and left there to these policemen who were on duty that night at the entrance to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the room that you were taken into, the size of the room and physically -- a physical description of the room, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: The room was roughly 3 metres by 5 in size. There was nothing in particular inside. There was a small window high up on the wall. At the entrance to that room, there was no door. There was just concrete on the floor. And I was put there with nothing in it, in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any furniture in the room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you alone in the room, or were there other people being kept in that room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I arrived, there was no one; I was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in this room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That night was the worst night of my life. After they had left me in that room, they started taking it out on me, both psychologically and physically abusing me. They told me to take off my clothes; I did so. And after I had stripped and when I was completely naked, they started beating me with various objects. They kicked me. They hit me with their fists. Then they brought some sort of a chair, then a bar. And so they beat me, until at one point I fainted. When I came to, they ordered me to go to the room next door. And there was a shower there. It was a kind of toilet or a bathroom of sorts. And they turned on the cold water for me to regain consciousness, after which they gave me some clothes that they found there. They gave me a pair of trousers and a shirt, which I put on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you made reference to "they," the people who mistreated you. How many people participated in this beating?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I am able to remember now, I think there were three or four of them who happened to be in that room at the time, three or four soldiers with white belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained in this room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in that room until the morning, throughout the night. And when it dawned, I was alone, lying on the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps -- perhaps my question wasn't clear. For what period of time were you kept in this room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to that night or generally, how much time I stayed there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the total duration of time that you were detained in this room.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I understand your question now. I was kept in that room for some 50 days or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the 50 days or so that you were detained in this room, were you able to become aware of which unit or units the military police who mistreated you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. In the course of those 50 days that I spent in that room, I found out from the guards and also from other people who subjected me to an investigation later on that since at the time they called themselves Krajiska police and that it was mostly the members of that Krajiska police. But as to what brigade, what unit they belonged to exactly, I never found out really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this first night, this beating that you've described for the Chamber, do you have any idea how long that period of beating took place on that first night?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That first night, as I've said already, they beat me up so badly that I fainted, whereupon they did not beat me again on that same night. But the beatings and the physical and psychological abuse went on for the entire duration, for all of those 50 days. For the most part it happened when I was being interrogated and also in the evenings, when I had to use the toilet or when I asked for a drink of water, either for myself or for my colleague, who was also brought to my cell after a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How frequently did these beatings occur?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of that 50-day period, I think that almost every evening I was hit several times or kicked. They beat me with their fists. Mostly the guards who were on duty that particular night. And it normally tended to happen in the evenings, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, Witness, that this room did not have a door on it. Did there come a time when a door was put on that room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That room where I found myself was later supplied with a door. And as far as I can remember, maybe six or seven days after I arrived, they put bars on the door as well as a proper door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you also told us that a colleague was brought into the cell after a certain period of time. Do you recall how many days passed before your colleague was brought into the cell?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: About 30 days had gone by when he was brought to that cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of your colleague who was brought into that cell with you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do remember well, since he is living in Vitez today. His name is Pero Samija, and he was found at Travnik hospital. He was wounded. He had been wounded in Vitez, and then he was transferred to Travnik. But that was before the major conflicts were taking place in the area of Travnik. And after greater problems, after bigger conflicts, he found himself as a patient in the hospital at Travnik, and so he couldn't go back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, Witness, that you were interrogated. Do you recall the number of times that you were interrogated while you were detained in this room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the first time that you were interrogated? And can you describe that for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: The first interrogation happened straight on the first morning, the following morning. I was interrogated -- as far as I could tell, I was interrogated by the head of the department or whatever, some sort of boss of that military police. And they were the ones guarding the entrance to the barracks of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of questions were you asked by this military police officer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the general information, name and so on. And then for the most part he asked me what military unit or formation I belonged to; how many soldiers were in the unit; how many people were armed in the city of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the interrogator do with the information that you provided to him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They were writing it down, and that statement that they took from me, well, I suppose he submitted it to the other officer who came to subject me to another more detailed interrogation after a few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you on that or any other occasion while you were detained at the Travnik barracks sign any statements?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had to sign that statement because there was always a policeman next to me with a bat, and I had no choice basically. I had to sign the statement I gave to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall any of the specific details about the second time you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was interrogated the second time, the first thing I remarked was that the person taking my statement was much more of an expert in interrogation techniques, because at the end of my statement he himself said to me that he was a legal expert by profession, that he was a law graduate, and that he was from the area of Krajina. And more specifically, I'd like to stress that when I was giving him my statement, at one point my former fellow student from primary school, Mujezinovic, came in. I think his first name is Enver. And he must have heard that I was in Travnik. And in a rather rough way, he told me, "Now you are going to see. Once we take Vitez, we will kill all the babies still in their mother's bellies." And this had an effect on me. It had a frightening effect on me, since I knew that guy, Mujezinovic, rather well, and I had never thought he was such an extreme nationalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of clothing was Enver Mujezinovic wearing when he said these words to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing his uniform, his standard uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to determine which army or military unit he was in by looking at his uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't do so at the time. I couldn't assess exactly what unit he would have belonged to. But I believed and I saw quite clearly that he had the lilies insignia of the BH army on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the person with the law training who was conducting this interview, what type of clothing was that person wearing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: He, too, was wearing a uniform, a shirt. And since he was an office-worker, he only wore a shirt and a pair of trousers. And obviously, he had the BH army insignia on his shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know this individual's name or perhaps which military unit he was assigned to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know the person's name, and I did not know what unit he belonged to, but I was aware of the fact that in that area the 3rd Corps - or perhaps the 7th Corps, as it had been changed afterwards - was active in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber about the third instance in which you were interrogated while detained in that room at the Travnik barracks.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 50 days that I spent in that room next to the gates or the entrance to the barracks -- once again, one of the members of the investigation team from the BH army came and took me to a place about 100 metres away inside the barracks, in another building. And later on, I learned that his name was Kasim and that prior to the start of the hostilities, he used to work at the police station in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were taken to this place inside the barracks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: He himself entered the room, and he said his name was Kasim, and he asked me to follow him. At that stage I didn't know where he was taking me to, but later on I saw he took me to a building within the perimeter of the barracks and he took me to a room where there was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander of that detention centre. His name was Jugo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were taken into the room with this person known as Jugo?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just one correction, sir, if I may. Jugo did not take me there. I got to that office accompanied by Kasim. So I entered the room where Jugo was sitting together with Kasim, and Jugo was the superior there. And then Jugo left the room, and I was left alone with Kasim who proceeded to take a statement from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any distinctive insignia or other indicators on Jugo's clothing as to which military unit he belonged?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Apart from the fact that he was wearing a uniform and he had those insignia of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know why you were interrogated on three different occasions while being detained in the Travnik barracks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to this day it is not clear to me why I was interrogated so many times. Perhaps it was because the very fact of taking me was a bit bizarre from their point of view, because I basically walked in on my own. And secondly, they thought I was perhaps one of the high-ranking officials within the HVO, since I was a law graduate and since I was a member of the military police. And they thought that by virtue of that very fact I was likely to provide them with a lot of information in relation to the situation, the combat readiness, and the information they were looking for. They were trying to find out as much as possible about the situation in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you in fact a high-ranking official within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was just an -- a member of the investigative team in the 4th Military Police. And as I did say earlier on, my only duty was investigating any infringements committed by the HVO members in the area covered by that unit. So no way was I a high-ranking official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you were detained on 7 August 1993, what was your rank, your military rank?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I had no rank at the time when I was taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the third interrogation by Kasim, where were you taken after that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: So once that interrogation was over, I myself -- actually, a couple of us, because I think -- no, I think there were about four or five of us soldiers from the HVO. We were taken to a place not far away from the barracks to the building of the former HVO government in Travnik, and that building is next to the hotel in Travnik. It was called the building next to the three pine trees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of these other four or five HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do recollect the names clearly. The soldiers who were with me were Dzidzic Ljiljan, Bobas -- just a moment. Krunoslav Bonic, Dzidzic Ljiljan, and then Zulj Stipo, and some of them stayed in Travnik, such as Slipac Nikica, Jelencic Zivko was another one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, prior to the time you were taken to the former HVO government building in Travnik, were you kept in any other rooms in the Travnik barracks compound, other than the room by the guardhouse where you stayed for 50 days?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So after the first interrogation on the part of Kasim, I was kept in a room of that building, in the basement, and I was put in a room where there were also soldiers of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in the room with the soldiers of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember how many days exactly, but I think I stayed there about 30 to 40 days in that room, together with the BH army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you later in a basement room in that building with other HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I was saying, after 30 to 40 days that I spent with the soldiers of the BH army, I was moved to a room where there were just the imprisoned HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people were detained in this room with you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, I can't tell you exactly. But I think there were about 10, maybe a dozen, 13 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were these the same soldiers whose names you provided to us a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those three or four that I've given you the names for. And there was some others as well, but right now I don't seem to be able to recollect the names. But those soldiers as well, the ones I mentioned before, were in that same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were kept in this basement room with these HVO soldiers, were you physically mistreated at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I myself, no. But I saw that other HVO soldiers were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber any of those incidents where other HVO soldiers were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I remember well one situation in particular, Krunoslav Bonic, who was the youngest in that room, well, one of the guards - I think his name was Mujo and he was from the area of Siprag, not very far from Travnik - and whenever he was on duty, he would take the above-mentioned Kruno out and he would beat him up so badly and sometimes even before our very eyes. And sometimes he would take him a bit further away to another room and we could hear his screams. And then he would bring him back to our room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the other individuals who were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I remember one occasion only, when Mr. Ivo Rajkovic, who was also brought to our room together with Ivo Fisic, and on his way back -- coming back from the toilet one of the BH army attacked him, kicked him very badly, hit him with his fist - and that before the eyes of the guards who were there to guard us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. This is approximately when we take our recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. We are going to have a technical break now. It is 10.30, and we shall continue with the hearing at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if it's going to be a problem again, but I didn't get French -- or English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. Everything's working now. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after you were detained in the -- how long were you detained in the basement of the barracks building in Travnik, in total?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly for how many days it was, but I do know that on the 24th of December, 1993 I was transferred from that basement to the KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the period that you were detained at the barracks compound, including at the gatehouse, was from 7 August 1993 until 24 December 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've also told us about being placed in the HVO building in town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in that location?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly the number of days I spent there, but I believe, as we have already said, that my sojourn in Travnik lasted from the 7th of August, 1993 until the 24th of December, 1993. Now, I cannot be precise as to the number of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as a result of the physical mistreatment that you received, do you have any lingering medical conditions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I do. They are mainly manifested in the form of frequent headaches, so that I need to take a painkiller or some sedatives to calm me down. So these are occasional health problems that I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before giving the floor to Defence counsel, I have a few minor points of clarification regarding your answers. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question was put to you regarding your professional career. You explained that you studied at the Faculty of Law and that after that you were employed in the cadastre of the Vitez municipality. And then I see the English text, which indicates this. And after that, you became an inspector in the fiscal administration. You worked there for about two years. And then according to what you said, it appears that for several years you held the position of a magistrate or a judge. Could you be more precise on this point. What did you do exactly? What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, what you have just said is quite correct, but let me just elaborate. My first job was in the cadastre, then two years as inspector for social revenues. And after that, I worked as a magistrate judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was inquiring about your work as a judge. So you were in charge of -- you acted as a judge for traffic violations.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: My exact title was Judge for Minor Offences Attached to Vitez Municipality, and I worked in that position for four or five years. This actually entailed offences against public law and order, so offences in the area of traffic, then offences in the sense of failure to pay taxes, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English text, it was indicated - and this may be an error of interpretation - that you were elected to this position of judge. There's the word "elected"; whereas later on you were appointed as head of the legal and administrative department. As a judge, were you elected or appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As regards appointments for -- to the position of judge, at the Municipal Council I was elected. There was a vacancy, a competition, and I was admitted to this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were elected and appointed. There was no proper election, was there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, there wasn't a vote. I applied for the post, and I was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in the English text, the word "elected" should be replaced with "appointed." So this is a minor point of precision. When you were a lawyer, you studied law. You even had a legal position. When you were detained - and you said in response to a question from the Prosecution that you were detained for several months - when you left prison, were you given a document indicating that you had been released? Were you given a document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I have to go back for a moment to the time when I was detained in Travnik. A legal proceedings were instituted against me, and two or three times I was interrogated in the military court and after statements, I was released. But I never received that document. But I learnt that the proceedings were halted and this was also published in a paper called Travnicki Ljiljani, and the public prosecutor, Mr. Sead Zeric, in his statement said that the proceedings against me were being dropped because there was no proof that I had committed any criminal offence. And I attached this to my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what were the charges against you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As it was stated in the criminal report, according to my recollection, the charge was armed rebellion, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for these clarifications that emanated from the examination-in-chief. Having made these remarks, I turn to the Defence to give them the floor for the cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I would like to ask you to be kind enough to answer some of my questions. Of course, you will answer to the best of your knowledge. You told the Trial Chamber that in 1992 -- let me rephrase it. Is it true that in June 1992 you were appointed chief of legal affairs within the Secretariat of the Interior of Vitez Municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer to that question because, as I said in my statement, I wasn't appointed chief of legal affairs. But upon the proposal of the then-head of the police station, Mr. Pero Skopljak, I was invited to an interview and asked whether I would accept that position. And I said I would, as I had been a judge for four or five years and I had had enough of that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in mid-1992, when you accepted the position offered to you, the internal affairs body was still working as a multi-ethnic body, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, already at the time, that is, in mid-1992 or the second half of 1992, you had already noticed certain signs of tension, particularly with respect to the engagement of individuals for the reserve police force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ID cards for the reserve police were -- gave those people other entitlements, such as the right to carry a weapon. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As regards engagement for the reserve police force, as far as I know, initially people were given uniforms, ID cards. And as for the details, now, whether weapons were issued, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, however, Mr. Josipovic, that in fact there was a certain kind of competition between the head, who was a Croat, and his deputy, the chief of the uniformed police, as to who would issue more ID cards to members of his own ethnic group? Was that the reason for the tensions that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. There were frequent disagreements between the head of the police station and the head of the uniformed police. That is when I noticed that the two of them would have some disputes as to why so many IDs were issued to so many people, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you just explained that. My question was that the tensions and the possibility of a conflict between the army and the HVO was one of the reasons why you formally joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Those tensions towards the end of 1992 increased to such a point that on both sides uniformed units started to be formed. And that is how I, too, decided at the beginning of November 1992 to join the HVO. To be more concrete, I joined the 4th Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said in response to a question from the Prosecutor, you worked as a crime investigator and your duties included investigations in the case of smuggling, theft, and occasionally murder.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Working in that area, you were not an ordinary soldier; you were actually an officer of the HVO without a particular rank, were you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't an officer. I was just an officer investigator in the criminal police. This was a section of the police whose main duties were to investigate criminal acts that may have been perpetrated by members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after you joined the HVO, overt conflicts started between the HVO and the BH army primarily in the areas of Kiseljak and Busovaca, and later in other areas as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of these conflicts and as a result of those conflicts, a large portion of the Bosniak Muslim population from Busovaca, Vitez, and Kiseljak left the area and most of them headed towards Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is a question I cannot answer in the affirmative because the largest conflicts that started in April 1993, I didn't notice one or other ethnic group departing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, most of the exodus occurred in April, after the massacre in Ahmici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the framework of your duties as a crime inspector, you said that you mostly investigated criminal acts, thefts, burglaries, and murders, the victims of which were members of the Croatian people and which occurred in the area under the control of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, as a military policeman of the HVO, you could not go to the areas under the control of the BH army to carry out any investigations there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, because the conflict had already started and it was dangerous and even impossible for one to carry out any investigations over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That applied in the opposite case too. The military police of the BH army couldn't come to Busovaca, Kiseljak, or Vitez to investigate things that it felt it should investigate. This applied to both sides, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After these large-scale conflicts, neither side had access to the other side or the areas controlled by the other side, to try and investigate over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the Prosecutor, by way of an example you said that your military police did not carry out any investigations in connection with events that you had heard had happened in Dusina and Miletici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know -- in fact, I'm quite certain that our military police, the military police I belonged to, did not go to Dusina or to Maljine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it true, Mr. Josipovic, that most of the inhabitants of those villages crossed to the area under HVO control and that their statements were taken by the security service, the so-called SIC? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you clarify that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Most of the inhabitants of Dusina and Miletici, which you mentioned as examples, after those events crossed to areas under HVO control and statements from those persons were taken by the security service of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I have no information about that, what you are referring to. So I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you gave a different answer regarding that matter in your statement given to the Prosecution, that means that you -- that you were misunderstood; is that right? Because in your statement you say that you heard of those events - this is paragraph 14 - "I do not remember ever taking a statement from the survivors. I think this was something the Security Intelligence Service handled, the SIS."

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I would just add: As stated in that statement, that I and the military police did not do that. Now, whether this was done by the SIS, I don't think I had any information about it, whether they did that or didn't. I cannot say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Also, your service and your military police also did not carry out any investigations after the massacre in Ahmici, did you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's right; we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Josipovic, that after that event a permanent and very hot combat lines were established between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council throughout the Lasva Valley? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the reason why you also moved from a building that was less safe, that is, from the Vitez Hotel, to a building that was safer.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Until large-scale hostilities broke out, that is, the events in Ahmici, we were based in the police station building. And after that, we were moved to the Vitez Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us now go back for a moment to this unfortunate event that you experienced and the things you told the Prosecutor about in answer to his question. As you said, on the 7th of August you were returning from duty and you took a wrong turning at a crossroads towards Vitez. When you were stopped by the BH army in territory under their control, you were wearing a uniform of the HVO and you were armed with a rifle and a pistol; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just then for them you were an enemy soldier whom they had captured; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It appears to be so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you stated, you were taken to the former JNA barracks in Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day -- or rather, the day after, your first interrogation was linked to military issues only. The investigator wanted to learn as much as possible about the strength and position of an army that was its enemy; at the time, that is the HVO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Travnik, your relative, Dijana Drazetic [phoen] resided.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: She is not a relative of mine. She is a magistrate judge in the court in Travnik when I was a judge in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, she learnt from you that you were in detention and she asked a pre-war acquaintance of yours and her colleague, Beker Ferizovic, the judge, to come and visit you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how she learnt -- or rather, how Mr. Beker Ferizovic learnt about it. Anyway, he did come, but he came after, certainly, more than 30 days of my detention had gone by, that is, from the moment I entered the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With Mr. Beker Ferizovic, you maintained good friendly relations to the present day; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I am still a good friend of Mr. Beker Ferizovic. We are still good friends, and we hear one another quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He visited you on a number of occasions, brought you food and clothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not. A part of your question is incorrect. He didn't bring food. He brought a pair of trousers and socks once or twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your lady acquaintance was also able to visit you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She came once, and we had a chat, and she didn't come again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, you said that you spent that first night in this room close to the entrance to the barracks and that there was nothing in the room except bare concrete. However, already the next day or the day after you were brought a soldier's cot.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, not a soldier's bed. Not even after seven or eight days. Some wooden planks were placed on the concrete floor and a blanket on that -- those planks. And then I was given another blanket to cover myself with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that room you spent -- on the concrete floor, you only spent that one night, the night of your arrest.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I spent 50-odd days in that room, as I said in my statement, which means I was in that room for some 50-odd days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe my question wasn't quite clear.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I meant to say was that it was only for that one night that you lay on the concrete. After that, you were brought those wooden planks and some days later you were given a soldier's bed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a few days afterwards I was brought a bed. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the President of the Trial Chamber, you explained that criminal proceedings were conducted against you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The charge was armed rebellion. You told us that just now, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a lawyer, you can confirm here in court that this charge is envisaged and described as a serious criminal offence in our Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a serious criminal offence, according to the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to our criminal procedure law, which was taken over from the former Yugoslavia, detention was compulsory; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to our law, detention in the course of investigation could last up to six months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Probably it's correct. I was not sufficiently familiar with all the provisions of that law, because I was a magistrate for minor offences. I was not a judge of a municipal court or anything. So I was not all that familiar with all the provisions of that law or even that particular definition of that crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the question put to you by the Prosecution, you replied that you spent some time in a cell together with some members of the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. And the members of the armed forces were imprisoned because they were under investigation due to accusations of stealing, looting, or murder; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of them was in fact a member of the armed forces who was accused of having killed two Croats in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a legal expert amongst people who are under investigation, you sometimes gave them possible advice about the procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that investigation and several interrogations you were subjected to were completed, you were brought before the court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were appointed a defence lawyer.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember a defence lawyer. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the investigation and your interrogation provided no basis for a trial, according to the legal proceedings the trial was suspended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereupon, as a prisoner of war, you were moved to the KP Dom, to Zenica by the end of December.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of December, I was moved to KP Dom Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were exchanged on the 22nd of March, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Josipovic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am turning to the other Defence team now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, we do not have any questions for this witness. Our client is not charged with any of the incidents that the witness has testified about, Your Honours. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to specify one point. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just said - I can see on the transcript in English - that you were transferred to KP Dom Zenica on the 24th of December and you were exchanged on the 22nd of March, 1994. Apparently that's the date when you left KP Dom Zenica. As you're a legal expert, I'm going to put a legal question to you: The detention between the 22nd of December,1993 until the 22nd of March, 1994 was for what legal reason, according to you? Because according to what you have said in reply to the questions put to you by the Defence, the charges against you were dropped before the 24th of December. So according to you, between the 24th of December until the -- and the 22nd of March, you were detained for what reason? Do you have an explanation for that or don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you just reformulate your question, be a bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. You have told us that you were under an investigation and you were brought before the court and the charges were dropped. One can deduce that once the charges are dropped, at that stage your detention should have been over. You told us that between the 24th of December -- that on the 24th of December you were transferred to Zenica prison. Did it indicate the end of your detention in connection to the charges brought against you? And if so, between December and March what was your situation? Can you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They decided to start criminal proceedings against me because they were convinced that I was a higher-ranking official than I was, since I was a university graduate, and before the war I was a magistrate. And they thought I would have a great deal of information that could -- that I could tell them. This was the key reason why they started these proceedings against me. But in the course of these proceedings, they ascertained that, well, I wasn't such a person and that up until the point when I was arrested I committed no crime at all. And so charges could not be brought against me and I could not be imprisoned. And that was perhaps the key moment when they decided to take me out of that prison in Travnik and move me to Zenica, because according to them it was a safer place or a place where the other prisoners were and the place from which they organised their exchanges of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm turning to the Prosecution. Do you have any additional questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a couple of questions arising from the cross-examination, if I might put those to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go on. Re-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, does the -- either the Bosnian Criminal Code or the SFRY Criminal Code authorise physical mistreatment or beating during periods of pre-trial detention?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: On no account. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to clarify one more point. On the occasion of my arrival to the district prison of Zenica, when I first arrived there, when I was being admitted there and handed over by the policeman who accompanied me, well, on that occasion I was physically abused as well. So on the back of my body -- well, I was hit in the back, behind my right ear, so that I still suffer the consequences of that. This is just one more clarification. And that was the only time I was hit at the district prison in Zenica. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Considering the fact that the witness is sharing this fact with us of his own free will, would you like to ask any questions of him on this point? Further cross-examination by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct, Mr. Josipovic, that the day after at KP Dom you were received by one of the heads there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was Mr. Alagic, who was the commander of the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you realised immediately that the person who hit you as you arrived was reported and sanctioned?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. The one who brought me there said -- no. The guy who hit me was tall, and he had a beard, and he was told, "This is not the way you treat prisoners," and so the other guy was really correct and that's what he said. But as to whether any proceedings were started against this, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was reported to the commander who listened to -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, he wasn't reported. It was just that the policeman who accompanied me there said to him that this was not the way to deal with prisoners. And it was in the evening. It was just a person who was on duty, and then some bearded guy came along and he hit me from behind. But as to whether he was reported to his superior, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. The Prosecution has no further questions. So we thank you for having come to The Hague to give us your testimony. You have answered to all the questions put to you by the Prosecution and the Defence and the Judges, so we thank you very much for this witness account. We wish you a pleasant return to your home. And I'm going to ask Madam Usher to take you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. According to our schedule, this is all, because all the witnesses planned for this week have given their witness accounts. As you know, there will be no session tomorrow due to maintenance reasons, and so we'll start tomorrow at 2.15 [as interpreted]. Let me just inform the Prosecution and the Defence that we have made a decision yesterday with reference to witnesses, the 92 bis, which should have been at 15.50 or so, the decision should have been recorded at that time. As I have mentioned, we still have the request with regard to the admission of these facts. The decision will be made as soon as we have all the relevant elements in order to be able to deliberate. Apart from that, we are looking forward to receiving a written request with regard to the points you have mentioned earlier on with regard to ambiguities or gaps in the regulation which might work against you in the course of these proceedings. So we expect you to make these requests in writing and then we'll reply. Since this is all, the session is over and we can all come back here at quarter past 2.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.44 a.m.,
